chunks: Humayd ibn Ziyad from al-Hasan ibn Muhammad al-Kindi, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Mithami, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Nu'man al-Razi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

The people fled on the Day of Uhud from the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), so he became angry with intense anger. He said: 'And whenever he became angry, sweat would descend from his forehead like pearls.'

So he looked and found Ali (peace be upon him) by his side, so he said to him: 'Go with the sons of your father to those who fled from the Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I have an example in you.' He said: 'So suffice for me against these.' So he charged and struck the first one he met from them. Jibraeel (peace be upon him) said: 'This is the consolation, O Muhammad.' He said: 'He is from me and I am from him.' Jibraeel (peace be upon him) said: 'And I am from you both, O Muhammad.'

So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) looked at Jibraeel (peace be upon him) on a throne of gold between the sky and the earth, and he was saying: 'There is no sword except Dhu al-Fiqar, and no young warrior except Ali.'

key_terms.ذُو الْفَقَار: Possessor of the Split Sword (epithet of Ali)

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of the phrase 'La saifa illa Dhu al-Fiqar' in Shia tradition?
ai.summary: This narration from *Al-Kafi* highlights the spiritual intimacy (*muwasah*) between the Prophet and Imam Ali during the Battle of Uhud, where Ali’s charge served as divine consolation for the Prophet’s distress over the archers' defection. It culminates in the Archangel Jibraeel witnessing the celestial declaration of 'No sword but Dhu al-Faqar, no youth but Ali,' a key text for Shia exegesis of Ali’s unique martial and spiritual status. The incident underscores the concept of *Tawalli* (divine love and alliance) as a source of strength in times of trial.
